**Surat al-Layl (The Night)** is Meccan and has twenty-one verses.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿By the night when it covers,﴾ ﴿and by the day when it becomes bright,﴾ ﴿and by Him who created the male and the female,﴾ ﴿indeed your efforts are diverse.﴾ ﴿As for him who gives and fears God,﴾ ﴿and confirms the best reward,﴾ ﴿We will ease him toward ease.﴾ ﴿But as for him who is stingy and considers himself self-sufficient,﴾ ﴿and denies the best reward,﴾ ﴿We will ease him toward hardship.﴾ ﴿And his wealth will not avail him when he falls.﴾ ﴿Indeed, upon Us is guidance.﴾ ﴿And indeed, to Us belong the Hereafter and the first life.﴾ ﴿So I have warned you of a Fire that blazes,﴾ ﴿none will enter it except the most wretched,﴾ ﴿who denies and turns away.﴾ ﴿But the most righteous will be spared from it,﴾ ﴿who gives his wealth to purify himself,﴾ ﴿and no one has any favour with him for which he must be repaid,﴾ ﴿except seeking the countenance of his Lord, the Most High.﴾ ﴿And he will surely be well-pleased.﴾

This surah is Meccan. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥa said it is Madinan, and it was said that it contains a Madinan verse. When [the surah] mentioned in the previous one, ﴿He has succeeded who purifies it, and he has failed who corrupts it﴾ [al-Shams: 9–10], it here mentions the attributes by which success is attained and those by which failure is incurred. Then it warns of the Fire and mentions who will enter it and who will avoid it. The object of "yaghshā" (covers) is omitted, so it may refer to the day, as in His words, ﴿He covers the night over the day﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 54], or to the sun, as in His words, ﴿By the night when it covers it﴾ [al-Shams: 4]. It was also said that it refers to the earth and everything in it [being covered] by its darkness. "Tajallā" means it became unveiled and manifest, either by the departure of the darkness of the night or by the light of the sun. He swears by the night, in which every living creature returns to its resting place, and by the day, in which they disperse. The poet said:

"It unveils the journey from its face, over a smooth [rock] on the way, bright, its fat abundant."

The majority read "tajallā" as a past-tense verb whose subject is a pronoun referring to the day. ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr read "tatajallā" with two tāʾs, meaning the sun. It was also read "tujlā" with a ḍamma on the tāʾ and sukūn on the jīm, meaning the sun.

(Wa mā khalaqa): "mā" is either a verbal-source particle (maṣdariyya) or means "alladhī" (who). The apparent meaning is the generality of the male and the female. It was said that it refers only to the children of Adam, because they are specially connected to God's guardianship and obedience. Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Kalbī and al-Ḥasan said that they are Adam and Ḥawwāʾ. The established reading in the codices of the metropolitan cities, which is mass-transmitted (mutawātir), is ﴿and Him who created the male and the female﴾. What is transmitted in a ḥadīth as a reading, "wal-dhakari wal-unthā," is a solitary report (naql āḥād) that contradicts the consonantal text (sawād), so it is not counted as Qur'an. Thaʿlab mentioned that some of the early generation read "wa mā khalaqa al-dhakari" with the genitive on "dhakar," and al-Zamakhsharī cited it from al-Kisāʾī. It has been explained as an apposition (badal) to "mā," with the implied meaning "and He who created the male and the female." It may also be explained as an influence of the verbal noun, meaning "and the creation of the male and the female," as the poet said:

"The seekers of gifts circle around his doors, as the monk circles the church."

Here "al-rāhib" is in the genitive because of the implied utterance of the verbal noun: he saw [it] like the monk's circling of the church.

﴿Indeed your efforts﴾, that is, your endeavours, ﴿are diverse﴾, scattered and varied. Then it details this effort: ﴿As for him who gives﴾, the verse [continues]. It is reported that it was revealed about Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, may God be pleased with him, who used to free his weak slaves who had embraced Islam, and spend his wealth seeking the pleasure of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), while the disbelievers were the opposite of him. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Awfā said: this surah was revealed about Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, may God be pleased with him, and Abū Sufyān ibn Ḥarb. al-Suddī said: it was revealed about Abū al-Dahdāḥ al-Anṣārī, because of what he used to hang in the mosque as charity, and because of the palm tree he bought from a hypocrite in exchange for a garden of his. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) had bargained with the hypocrite over buying it, offering in exchange a palm tree in Paradise. This was because of orphans whose house the palm tree overlooked; things would fall from it and the orphans would take them, but the hypocrite prevented them, and refused [to sell]. Abū al-Dahdāḥ came and said: "O Messenger of God, I will buy the palm tree that is in Paradise for this one." The two objects of "aʿṭā" (gave) are omitted, since the intent is praise of the giver, without focusing on the recipient or the gift. Its apparent meaning is spending wealth in what is obligatory, recommended, or noble. Qatāda said: "gave" means gave God's right. Ibn Zayd said: he spent his wealth in God's way. ﴿And fears﴾: Ibn ʿAbbās said: he feared God. Mujāhid said: he feared stinginess. Qatāda said: he refrained from what was forbidden.

﴿And confirms the best reward﴾: "al-ḥusnā" is the feminine form of "al-aḥsan" (the best). Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrima and a group said: it is the testimony in this world, which God's promise is conveyed with. Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan and a group said: it is Paradise. A group said: it is the reward. al-Sulamī and others said: there is no god but God.

﴿We will ease him toward ease﴾, that is, We will prepare him for the state that is easiest and least difficult for him, both in this world and the Hereafter. He contrasted "gives" with "is stingy," and "fears" with "considers himself self-sufficient," because he renounced what is with God by saying "considers himself self-sufficient." ﴿Toward hardship﴾ is the evil state in this world and the Hereafter. al-Zamakhsharī said: "We will forsake him and withhold from him the divine favours until obedience becomes the most difficult and most arduous thing for him," like His words, ﴿He makes his breast narrow and constricted, as if he were climbing into the sky﴾ [al-Anʿām: 125]. He named the path of good "ease," because its outcome is ease, and the path of evil "hardship," because its outcome is hardship. Or he meant by them the two paths of Paradise and Hell, meaning: "We will guide them both in the Hereafter to the two paths." End of his words. At the beginning of his speech there is a hint of Muʿtazilite doctrine. ﴿We will ease him toward hardship﴾ comes as a counterpart to ﴿We will ease him toward ease,﴾ though hardship has no easing in it, and "tayssīr" may be used to mean preparation, which occurs in both ease and hardship.

﴿And his wealth will not avail him﴾: "mā" may be a negative particle or an interrogative, meaning: "And what will his wealth avail him?" ﴿When he falls﴾: from "tardā" (taʿaffala) from "radā," meaning perished. Mujāhid said this. Qatāda and Abū Ṣāliḥ said: he fell into Hell, that is, fell from its edges. Some people said: he will be wrapped in his shroud, from "radā." Mālik ibn al-Dhi'b said:

"My place of rest was pierced with the tips of spears, and [my] cloak was returned over my eyes, the excess of my mantle."

Another said:

"Your portion of all that time gathers is two shrouds, in which you are wrapped, and camphor."

﴿Indeed upon Us is guidance﴾: this means making the path known and granting them perception, as He said: ﴿And upon God is the direction of the way﴾ [al-Naḥl: 9]. al-Zamakhsharī said: guiding to the truth is obligatory upon Us, by setting up proofs and explaining the laws.

﴿And indeed to Us belong the Hereafter and the first life﴾, that is, the reward of both abodes, in accordance with His words: ﴿We gave him his reward in this world, and indeed in the Hereafter he is among the righteous﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt: 27]. Ibn al-Zubayr, Zayd ibn ʿAlī, Ṭalḥa, Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna and ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr read "tatalaẓẓā" with two tāʾs. al-Bazzī read it with one doubled tāʾ, and the majority with one tāʾ. al-Zamakhsharī said: the verse is included in a comparison between two great states, one of the polytheists and one of the believers, so the aim is to emphasise their two contrasting attributes. So it says "al-ashqā" (the most wretched) and makes him exclusively for burning, as if the Fire had not been created except for him. And it says "al-atqā" (the most righteous) and makes him exclusively for salvation, as if Paradise had not been created except for him. It was said that they are Abū Jahl or Umayya ibn Khalaf, and Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, may God be pleased with him. "Yatazakkā" is from "zakāh" (purification), meaning he seeks to be purified before God, not intending by it showing off or reputation; or it is a verb of the form tafaʿʿala from "zakāh." He said this, but it is a forced grammatical analysis. "Tujzā" came in the passive voice because it is a rhyme-ending (fāṣila), and its original form was "najzihi iyyāhā" or "najziha iyyāhu." The majority read "illā ibtighāʾa" with a fatḥa on the hamza, and it is an exceptive construction that is disconnected (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ), because it is not included in "min niʿma" (any favour). ﴿By the night when it covers,﴾ ﴿and by the day when it becomes bright,﴾ ﴿and by Him who created the male and the female,﴾ ﴿indeed your efforts are diverse.﴾ ﴿As for him who gives and fears God,﴾ ﴿and confirms the best reward,﴾ ﴿We will ease him toward ease.﴾ ﴿But as for him who is stingy and considers himself self-sufficient,﴾ ﴿and denies the best reward,﴾ ﴿We will ease him toward hardship.﴾ ﴿And his wealth will not avail him when he falls.﴾ ﴿Indeed, upon Us is guidance.﴾ ﴿And indeed, to Us belong the Hereafter and the first life.﴾ ﴿So I have warned you of a Fire that blazes,﴾ ﴿none will enter it except the most wretched,﴾ ﴿who denies and turns away.﴾ ﴿But the most righteous will be spared from it,﴾ ﴿who gives his wealth to purify himself,﴾ ﴿and no one has any favour with him for which he must be repaid,﴾ ﴿except seeking the countenance of his Lord, the Most High.﴾ ﴿And he will surely be well-pleased.﴾

This surah is Meccan. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥa said it is Madinan, and it was said that it contains a Madinan verse. When [the surah] mentioned in the previous one, ﴿He has succeeded who purifies it, and he has failed who corrupts it﴾ [al-Shams: 9–10], it here mentions the attributes by which success is attained and those by which failure is incurred. Then it warns of the Fire and mentions who will enter it and who will avoid it. The object of "yaghshā" (covers) is omitted, so it may refer to the day, as in His words, ﴿He covers the night over the day﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 54], or to the sun, as in His words, ﴿By the night when it covers it﴾ [al-Shams: 4]. It was also said that it refers to the earth and everything in it [being covered] by its darkness. "Tajallā" means it became unveiled and manifest, either by the departure of the darkness of the night or by the light of the sun. He swears by the night, in which every living creature returns to its resting place, and by the day, in which they disperse. The poet said:

"It unveils the journey from its face, over a smooth [rock] on the way, bright, its fat abundant."

The majority read "tajallā" as a past-tense verb whose subject is a pronoun referring to the day. ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr read "tatajallā" with two tāʾs, meaning the sun. It was also read "tujlā" with a ḍamma on the tāʾ and sukūn on the jīm, meaning the sun.

(Wa mā khalaqa): "mā" is either a verbal-source particle (maṣdariyya) or means "alladhī" (who). The apparent meaning is the generality of the male and the female. It was said that it refers only to the children of Adam, because they are specially connected to God's guardianship and obedience. Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Kalbī and al-Ḥasan said that they are Adam and Ḥawwāʾ. The established reading in the codices of the metropolitan cities, which is mass-transmitted (mutawātir), is ﴿and Him who created the male and the female﴾. What is transmitted in a ḥadīth as a reading, "wal-dhakari wal-unthā," is a solitary report (naql āḥād) that contradicts the consonantal text (sawād), so it is not counted as Qur'an. Thaʿlab mentioned that some of the early generation read "wa mā khalaqa al-dhakari" with the genitive on "dhakar," and al-Zamakhsharī cited it from al-Kisāʾī. It has been explained as an apposition (badal) to "mā," with the implied meaning "and He who created the male and the female." It may also be explained as an influence of the verbal noun, meaning "and the creation of the male and the female," as the poet said:

"The seekers of gifts circle around his doors, as the monk circles the church."

Here "al-rāhib" is in the genitive because of the implied utterance of the verbal noun: he saw [it] like the monk's circling of the church.

﴿Indeed your efforts﴾, that is, your endeavours, ﴿are diverse﴾, scattered and varied. Then it details this effort: ﴿As for him who gives﴾, the verse [continues]. It is reported that it was revealed about Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, may God be pleased with him, who used to free his weak slaves who had embraced Islam, and spend his wealth seeking the pleasure of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), while the disbelievers were the opposite of him. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Awfā said: this surah was revealed about Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, may God be pleased with him, and Abū Sufyān ibn Ḥarb. al-Suddī said: it was revealed about Abū al-Dahdāḥ al-Anṣārī, because of what he used to hang in the mosque as charity, and because of the palm tree he bought from a hypocrite in exchange for a garden of his. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) had bargained with the hypocrite over buying it, offering in exchange a palm tree in Paradise. This was because of orphans whose house the palm tree overlooked; things would fall from it and the orphans would take them, but the hypocrite prevented them, and refused [to sell]. Abū al-Dahdāḥ came and said: "O Messenger of God, I will buy the palm tree that is in Paradise for this one." The two objects of "aʿṭā" (gave) are omitted, since the intent is praise of the giver, without focusing on the recipient or the gift. Its apparent meaning is spending wealth in what is obligatory, recommended, or noble. Qatāda said: "gave" means gave God's right. Ibn Zayd said: he spent his wealth in God's way. ﴿And fears﴾: Ibn ʿAbbās said: he feared God. Mujāhid said: he feared stinginess. Qatāda said: he refrained from what was forbidden.

﴿And confirms the best reward﴾: "al-ḥusnā" is the feminine form of "al-aḥsan" (the best). Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrima and a group said: it is the testimony in this world, which God's promise is conveyed with. Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan and a group said: it is Paradise. A group said: it is the reward. al-Sulamī and others said: there is no god but God.

﴿We will ease him toward ease﴾, that is, We will prepare him for the state that is easiest and least difficult for him, both in this world and the Hereafter. He contrasted "gives" with "is stingy," and "fears" with "considers himself self-sufficient," because he renounced what is with God by saying "considers himself self-sufficient." ﴿Toward hardship﴾ is the evil state in this world and the Hereafter. al-Zamakhsharī said: "We will forsake him and withhold from him the divine favours until obedience becomes the most difficult and most arduous thing for him," like His words, ﴿He makes his breast narrow and constricted, as if he were climbing into the sky﴾ [al-Anʿām: 125]. He named the path of good "ease," because its outcome is ease, and the path of evil "hardship," because its outcome is hardship. Or he meant by them the two paths of Paradise and Hell, meaning: "We will guide them both in the Hereafter to the two paths." End of his words. At the beginning of his speech there is a hint of Muʿtazilite doctrine. ﴿We will ease him toward hardship﴾ comes as a counterpart to ﴿We will ease him toward ease,﴾ though hardship has no easing in it, and "tayssīr" may be used to mean preparation, which occurs in both ease and hardship.

﴿And his wealth will not avail him﴾: "mā" may be a negative particle or an interrogative, meaning: "And what will his wealth avail him?" ﴿When he falls﴾: from "tardā" (taʿaffala) from "radā," meaning perished. Mujāhid said this. Qatāda and Abū Ṣāliḥ said: he fell into Hell, that is, fell from its edges. Some people said: he will be wrapped in his shroud, from "radā." Mālik ibn al-Dhi'b said:

"My place of rest was pierced with the tips of spears, and [my] cloak was returned over my eyes, the excess of my mantle."

Another said:

"Your portion of all that time gathers is two shrouds, in which you are wrapped, and camphor."

﴿Indeed upon Us is guidance﴾: this means making the path known and granting them perception, as He said: ﴿And upon God is the direction of the way﴾ [al-Naḥl: 9]. al-Zamakhsharī said: guiding to the truth is obligatory upon Us, by setting up proofs and explaining the laws.

﴿And indeed to Us belong the Hereafter and the first life﴾, that is, the reward of both abodes, in accordance with His words: ﴿We gave him his reward in this world, and indeed in the Hereafter he is among the righteous﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt: 27]. Ibn al-Zubayr, Zayd ibn ʿAlī, Ṭalḥa, Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna and ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr read "tatalaẓẓā" with two tāʾs. al-Bazzī read it with one doubled tāʾ, and the majority with one tāʾ. al-Zamakhsharī said: the verse is included in a comparison between two great states, one of the polytheists and one of the believers, so the aim is to emphasise their two contrasting attributes. So it says "al-ashqā" (the most wretched) and makes him exclusively for burning, as if the Fire had not been created except for him. And it says "al-atqā" (the most righteous) and makes him exclusively for salvation, as if Paradise had not been created except for him. It was said that they are Abū Jahl or Umayya ibn Khalaf, and Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, may God be pleased with him. "Yatazakkā" is from "zakāh" (purification), meaning he seeks to be purified before God, not intending by it showing off or reputation; or it is a verb of the form tafaʿʿala from "zakāh." He said this, but it is a forced grammatical analysis. "Tujzā" came in the passive voice because it is a rhyme-ending (fāṣila), and its original form was "najzihi iyyāhā" or "najziha iyyāhu." The majority read "illā ibtighāʾa" with a fatḥa on the hamza, and it is an exceptive construction that is disconnected (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ), because it is not included in "min niʿma" (any favour). ﴿By the night when it covers,﴾ ﴿and by the day when it becomes bright,﴾ ﴿and by Him who created the male and the female,﴾ ﴿indeed your efforts are diverse.﴾ ﴿As for him who gives and fears God,﴾ ﴿and confirms the best reward,﴾ ﴿We will ease him toward ease.﴾ ﴿But as for him who is stingy and considers himself self-sufficient,﴾ ﴿and denies the best reward,﴾ ﴿We will ease him toward hardship.﴾ ﴿And his wealth will not avail him when he falls.﴾ ﴿Indeed, upon Us is guidance.﴾ ﴿And indeed, to Us belong the Hereafter and the first life.﴾ ﴿So I have warned you of a Fire that blazes,﴾ ﴿none will enter it except the most wretched,﴾ ﴿who denies and turns away.﴾ ﴿But the most righteous will be spared from it,﴾ ﴿who gives his wealth to purify himself,﴾ ﴿and no one has any favour with him for which he must be repaid,﴾ ﴿except seeking the countenance of his Lord, the Most High.﴾ ﴿And he will surely be well-pleased.﴾

This surah is Meccan. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥa said it is Madinan, and it was said that it contains a Madinan verse. When [the surah] mentioned in the previous one, ﴿He has succeeded who purifies it, and he has failed who corrupts it﴾ [al-Shams: 9–10], it here mentions the attributes by which success is attained and those by which failure is incurred. Then it warns of the Fire and mentions who will enter it and who will avoid it. The object of "yaghshā" (covers) is omitted, so it may refer to the day, as in His words, ﴿He covers the night over the day﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 54], or to the sun, as in His words, ﴿By the night when it covers it﴾ [al-Shams: 4]. It was also said that it refers to the earth and everything in it [being covered] by its darkness. "Tajallā" means it became unveiled and manifest, either by the departure of the darkness of the night or by the light of the sun. He swears by the night, in which every living creature returns to its resting place, and by the day, in which they disperse. The poet said:

"It unveils the journey from its face, over a smooth [rock] on the way, bright, its fat abundant."

The majority read "tajallā" as a past-tense verb whose subject is a pronoun referring to the day. ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr read "tatajallā" with two tāʾs, meaning the sun. It was also read "tujlā" with a ḍamma on the tāʾ and sukūn on the jīm, meaning the sun.

(Wa mā khalaqa): "mā" is either a verbal-source particle (maṣdariyya) or means "alladhī" (who). The apparent meaning is the generality of the male and the female. It was said that it refers only to the children of Adam, because they are specially connected to God's guardianship and obedience. Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Kalbī and al-Ḥasan said that they are Adam and Ḥawwāʾ. The established reading in the codices of the metropolitan cities, which is mass-transmitted (mutawātir), is ﴿and Him who created the male and the female﴾. What is transmitted in a ḥadīth as a reading, "wal-dhakari wal-unthā," is a solitary report (naql āḥād) that contradicts the consonantal text (sawād), so it is not counted as Qur'an. Thaʿlab mentioned that some of the early generation read "wa mā khalaqa al-dhakari" with the genitive on "dhakar," and al-Zamakhsharī cited it from al-Kisāʾī. It has been explained as an apposition (badal) to "mā," with the implied meaning "and He who created the male and the female." It may also be explained as an influence of the verbal noun, meaning "and the creation of the male and the female," as the poet said:

"The seekers of gifts circle around his doors, as the monk circles the church."

Here "al-rāhib" is in the genitive because of the implied utterance of the verbal noun: he saw [it] like the monk's circling of the church.

﴿Indeed your efforts﴾, that is, your endeavours, ﴿are diverse﴾, scattered and varied. Then it details this effort: ﴿As for him who gives﴾, the verse [continues]. It is reported that it was revealed about Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, may God be pleased with him, who used to free his weak slaves who had embraced Islam, and spend his wealth seeking the pleasure of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), while the disbelievers were the opposite of him. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Awfā said: this surah was revealed about Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, may God be pleased with him, and Abū Sufyān ibn Ḥarb. al-Suddī said: it was revealed about Abū al-Dahdāḥ al-Anṣārī, because of what he used to hang in the mosque as charity, and because of the palm tree he bought from a hypocrite in exchange for a garden of his. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) had bargained with the hypocrite over buying it, offering in exchange a palm tree in Paradise. This was because of orphans whose house the palm tree overlooked; things would fall from it and the orphans would take them, but the hypocrite prevented them, and refused [to sell]. Abū al-Dahdāḥ came and said: "O Messenger of God, I will buy the palm tree that is in Paradise for this one." The two objects of "aʿṭā" (gave) are omitted, since the intent is praise of the giver, without focusing on the recipient or the gift. Its apparent meaning is spending wealth in what is obligatory, recommended, or noble. Qatāda said: "gave" means gave God's right. Ibn Zayd said: he spent his wealth in God's way. ﴿And fears﴾: Ibn ʿAbbās said: he feared God. Mujāhid said: he feared stinginess. Qatāda said: he refrained from what was forbidden.

﴿And confirms the best reward﴾: "al-ḥusnā" is the feminine form of "al-aḥsan" (the best). Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrima and a group said: it is the testimony in this world, which God's promise is conveyed with. Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan and a group said: it is Paradise. A group said: it is the reward. al-Sulamī and others said: there is no god but God.

﴿We will ease him toward ease﴾, that is, We will prepare him for the state that is easiest and least difficult for him, both in this world and the Hereafter. He contrasted "gives" with "is stingy," and "fears" with "considers himself self-sufficient," because he renounced what is with God by saying "considers himself self-sufficient." ﴿Toward hardship﴾ is the evil state in this world and the Hereafter. al-Zamakhsharī said: "We will forsake him and withhold from him the divine favours until obedience becomes the most difficult and most arduous thing for him," like His words, ﴿He makes his breast narrow and constricted, as if he were climbing into the sky﴾ [al-Anʿām: 125]. He named the path of good "ease," because its outcome is ease, and the path of evil "hardship," because its outcome is hardship. Or he meant by them the two paths of Paradise and Hell, meaning: "We will guide them both in the Hereafter to the two paths." End of his words. At the beginning of his speech there is a hint of Muʿtazilite doctrine. ﴿We will ease him toward hardship﴾ comes as a counterpart to ﴿We will ease him toward ease,﴾ though hardship has no easing in it, and "tayssīr" may be used to mean preparation, which occurs in both ease and hardship.

﴿And his wealth will not avail him﴾: "mā" may be a negative particle or an interrogative, meaning: "And what will his wealth avail him?" ﴿When he falls﴾: from "tardā" (taʿaffala) from "radā," meaning perished. Mujāhid said this. Qatāda and Abū Ṣāliḥ said: he fell into Hell, that is, fell from its edges. Some people said: he will be wrapped in his shroud, from "radā." Mālik ibn al-Dhi'b said:

"My place of rest was pierced with the tips of spears, and [my] cloak was returned over my eyes, the excess of my mantle."

Another said:

"Your portion of all that time gathers is two shrouds, in which you are wrapped, and camphor."

﴿Indeed upon Us is guidance﴾: this means making the path known and granting them perception, as He said: ﴿And upon God is the direction of the way﴾ [al-Naḥl: 9]. al-Zamakhsharī said: guiding to the truth is obligatory upon Us, by setting up proofs and explaining the laws.

﴿And indeed to Us belong the Hereafter and the first life﴾, that is, the reward of both abodes, in accordance with His words: ﴿We gave him his reward in this world, and indeed in the Hereafter he is among the righteous﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt: 27]. Ibn al-Zubayr, Zayd ibn ʿAlī, Ṭalḥa, Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna and ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr read "tatalaẓẓā" with two tāʾs. al-Bazzī read it with one doubled tāʾ, and the majority with one tāʾ. al-Zamakhsharī said: the verse is included in a comparison between two great states, one of the polytheists and one of the believers, so the aim is to emphasise their two contrasting attributes. So it says "al-ashqā" (the most wretched) and makes him exclusively for burning, as if the Fire had not been created except for him. And it says "al-atqā" (the most righteous) and makes him exclusively for salvation, as if Paradise had not been created except for him. It was said that they are Abū Jahl or Umayya ibn Khalaf, and Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, may God be pleased with him. "Yatazakkā" is from "zakāh" (purification), meaning he seeks to be purified before God, not intending by it showing off or reputation; or it is a verb of the form tafaʿʿala from "zakāh." He said this, but it is a forced grammatical analysis. "Tujzā" came in the passive voice because it is a rhyme-ending (fāṣila), and its original form was "najzihi iyyāhā" or "najziha iyyāhu." The majority read "illā ibtighāʾa" with a fatḥa on the hamza, and it is an exceptive construction that is disconnected (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ), because it is not included in "min niʿma" (any favour). What is transmitted in a ḥadīth as a reading, "wal-dhakari wal-unthā," is a solitary report (naql āḥād) that contradicts the consonantal text (sawād), so it is not counted as Qur'an. Thaʿlab mentioned that some of the early generation read "wa mā khalaqa al-dhakari" with the genitive on "dhakar," and al-Zamakhsharī cited it from al-Kisāʾī. It has been explained as an apposition (badal) to "mā," with the implied meaning "and He who created the male and the female." It may also be explained as an influence of the verbal noun, meaning "and the creation of the male and the female," as the poet said:

"The seekers of gifts circle around his doors, as the monk circles the church."

Here "al-rāhib" is in the genitive because of the implied utterance of the verbal noun: he saw [it] like the monk's circling of the church.

﴿Indeed your efforts﴾, that is, your endeavours, ﴿are diverse﴾, scattered and varied. Then it details this effort: ﴿As for him who gives﴾, the verse [continues]. It is reported that it was revealed about Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, may God be pleased with him, who used to free his weak slaves who had embraced Islam, and spend his wealth seeking the pleasure of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), while the disbelievers were the opposite of him. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Awfā said: this surah was revealed about Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, may God be pleased with him, and Abū Sufyān ibn Ḥarb. al-Suddī said: it was revealed about Abū al-Dahdāḥ al-Anṣārī, because of what he used to hang in the mosque as charity, and because of the palm tree he bought from a hypocrite in exchange for a garden of his. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) had bargained with the hypocrite over buying it, offering in exchange a palm tree in Paradise. This was because of orphans whose house the palm tree overlooked; things would fall from it and the orphans would take them, but the hypocrite prevented them, and refused [to sell]. Abū al-Dahdāḥ came and said: "O Messenger of God, I will buy the palm tree that is in Paradise for this one." The two objects of "aʿṭā" (gave) are omitted, since the intent is praise of the giver, without focusing on the recipient or the gift. Its apparent meaning is spending wealth in what is obligatory, recommended, or noble. Qatāda said: "gave" means gave God's right. Ibn Zayd said: he spent his wealth in God's way. ﴿And fears﴾: Ibn ʿAbbās said: he feared God. Mujāhid said: he feared stinginess. Qatāda said: he refrained from what was forbidden.

﴿And confirms the best reward﴾: "al-ḥusnā" is the feminine form of "al-aḥsan" (the best). Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrima and a group said: it is the testimony in this world, which God's promise is conveyed with. Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan and a group said: it is Paradise. A group said: it is the reward. al-Sulamī and others said: there is no god but God.

﴿We will ease him toward ease﴾, that is, We will prepare him for the state that is easiest and least difficult for him, both in this world and the Hereafter. He contrasted "gives" with "is stingy," and "fears" with "considers himself self-sufficient," because he renounced what is with God by saying "considers himself self-sufficient." ﴿Toward hardship﴾ is the evil state in this world and the Hereafter. al-Zamakhsharī said: "We will forsake him and withhold from him the divine favours until obedience becomes the most difficult and most arduous thing for him," like His words, ﴿He makes his breast narrow and constricted, as if he were climbing into the sky﴾ [al-Anʿām: 125]. He named the path of good "ease," because its outcome is ease, and the path of evil "hardship," because its outcome is hardship. Or he meant by them the two paths of Paradise and Hell, meaning: "We will guide them both in the Hereafter to the two paths." End of his words. At the beginning of his speech there is a hint of Muʿtazilite doctrine. ﴿We will ease him toward hardship﴾ comes as a counterpart to ﴿We will ease him toward ease,﴾ though hardship has no easing in it, and "tayssīr" may be used to mean preparation, which occurs in both ease and hardship.

﴿And his wealth will not avail him﴾: "mā" may be a negative particle or an interrogative, meaning: "And what will his wealth avail him?" ﴿When he falls﴾: from "tardā" (taʿaffala) from "radā," meaning perished. Mujāhid said this. Qatāda and Abū Ṣāliḥ said: he fell into Hell, that is, fell from its edges. Some people said: he will be wrapped in his shroud, from "radā." Mālik ibn al-Dhi'b said:

"My place of rest was pierced with the tips of spears, and [my] cloak was returned over my eyes, the excess of my mantle."

Another said:

"Your portion of all that time gathers is two shrouds, in which you are wrapped, and camphor."

﴿Indeed upon Us is guidance﴾: this means making the path known and granting them perception, as He said: ﴿And upon God is the direction of the way﴾ [al-Naḥl: 9]. al-Zamakhsharī said: guiding to the truth is obligatory upon Us, by setting up proofs and explaining the laws.

﴿And indeed to Us belong the Hereafter and the first life﴾, that is, the reward of both abodes, in accordance with His words: ﴿We gave him his reward in this world, and indeed in the Hereafter he is among the righteous﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt: 27]. Ibn al-Zubayr, Zayd ibn ʿAlī, Ṭalḥa, Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna and ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr read "tatalaẓẓā" with two tāʾs. al-Bazzī read it with one doubled tāʾ, and the majority with one tāʾ. al-Zamakhsharī said: the verse is included in a comparison between two great states, one of the polytheists and one of the believers, so the aim is to emphasise their two contrasting attributes. So it says "al-ashqā" (the most wretched) and makes him exclusively for burning, as if the Fire had not been created except for him. And it says "al-atqā" (the most righteous) and makes him exclusively for salvation, as if Paradise had not been created except for him. It was said that they are Abū Jahl or Umayya ibn Khalaf, and Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, may God be pleased with him. "Yatazakkā" is from "zakāh" (purification), meaning he seeks to be purified before God, not intending by it showing off or reputation; or it is a verb of the form tafaʿʿala from "zakāh." End of his words.

The majority read "yatazakkā" as the present tense of "tazakkā." al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may God be pleased with them all, read it with assimilation of the tāʾ into the zāy. "Yatazakkā" is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), so its place in grammar is accusative. al-Zamakhsharī permitted that it has no place in grammatical analysis (iʿrāb), because he made it a substitute for the relative clause of "alladhī," which is "yu'tī" (gives). He said this, but it is a forced grammatical analysis. "Tujzā" came in the passive voice because it is a rhyme-ending (fāṣila), and its original form was "najzihi iyyāhā" or "najziha iyyāhu." The majority read "illā ibtighāʾa" with a fatḥa on the hamza, and it is an exceptive construction that is disconnected (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ), because it is not included in "min niʿma" (any favour). Ibn Wathhāb read it with a ḍamma as a substitute in the position of "niʿma," because it is in the nominative case, and this is the dialect of Tamīm. He cited both readings with the verse of Bishr ibn Abī Ḥāzim:

"They became empty, barren wastes, with no companion in them, except the wild cows, and the darknesses alternate."

And the rajaz poet, in the nominative:

"And a land in which there is no companion, except the wild oxen, and except the she-camels."

Ibn Abī ʿAbla read "illā ibtighā" with a shortened ending. al-Zamakhsharī said: "ibtighāʾa wajhi Allāh" may also be a verbal object of purpose (mafʿūl lahu) in meaning, because the meaning of the speech is: he gives his wealth only seeking the countenance of his Lord, not to repay His favours. End of his words. He took this from the words of al-Farrāʾ, who said: it is accusative by interpreting it as "what I give you seeking your reward," rather, "seeking the countenance of God."

﴿And he will surely be well-pleased﴾: a promise of the reward with which he will be pleased. The majority read "yarḍā" with a fatḥa on the yāʾ. It was also read with a ḍamma on it, meaning he is pleased with his own act, which God is pleased with and rewards him for.
